description:
I'm Juan Alberto, a computer educator from Argentina. I build full-stack apps, integrate hardware/AI, and create 3D prototypes. As a robotics mentor, I guide teams from idea to functional prototype in an organized, welcoming environment.

Join my team to build a solid solution together!
summary: Fire History Interface is a bilingual web platform that gives Argentina a continuous record of fire hot spots from 2000 to today. The challenge is that NASA’s two fire sensors do not count alike: MODIS, with 1 km pixels, sees about 3.3 times fewer hot spots than VIIRS, with 375 m pixels. Stitching the two series together creates a false jump in 2012. Our pipeline downloads NASA FIRMS data, removes fixed industrial heat sources and assigns detections to 5 × 5 km cells. It then converts MODIS to the VIIRS scale with factors per province and month. These factors are calibrated on days when every satellite was operating and stabilized with hierarchical shrinkage. Every month is tagged as observed, mixed or estimated, and carries an 80% uncertainty range and a confidence level. In leave-one-year-out validation, the national annual total is off by 4.2% on average. A FastAPI service and a React map let users explore calendars, compare any month with its historical normal and download data. As an extra, we added an experimental 24-hour fire-risk model (ROC-AUC 0.92). The result is a transparent, reproducible baseline for fire monitoring and early warning.
details:
What it does
Fire History Interface turns 26 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent, explorable record for Argentina. Users choose a province, a region or any area on the map and get a monthly calendar from November 2000 to today. They can also compare any month with its historical normal, inspect 5 × 5 km cells on an animated map and download the data.

How it works

  1. Pipeline (Python). It downloads NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m data, both the standard archive and near real time.
    • It removes fixed heat sources such as gas flares and industry: 478 points detected by night-time persistence and the FIRMS type = 2 flag.
    • It assigns every detection to a national grid of 112,711 cells and records which satellites were operating each day.
    • For each province and calendar month we compute a VIIRS/MODIS factor, using only days when every satellite was operating.
    • Hierarchical shrinkage (province → region → country) keeps the factor stable where there are few fires.
    • Before 2012, or on any day VIIRS was down, the value is estimated as MODIS × factor. Every month is labeled observed, mixed or estimated, with an 80% range and a high, medium or low confidence level.
  2. API (FastAPI + DuckDB over Parquet). It serves calendars, series, anomalies, map cells and downloads. It runs no machine learning: it only reads published tables, so every number can be audited.
  3. Interface (React + TypeScript + MapLibre). It is fully bilingual, works on phones and with the keyboard, and has a “How is it calculated?” dialog that shows the formula with a worked example.

Validation

  • We reproduced the published factors exactly.
  • We tested the method on years left out of the fit. The national annual total is off by 4.2% on average (worst year: 11%), and the province-month error is 14.8%.
  • We report the method’s weak points openly. For example, the ranges cover 77% instead of 80% in a forward test. We documented these limits in the API, and the anomaly is now computed within each sensor era.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Firefighters, provincial emergency agencies and planners can see whether a season is unusual by comparing it with a fair baseline, instead of a record distorted by the sensor change.
    • Córdoba, September 2020: 12.3 times the median. The guide links to official SNMF and CONAE burned-area sources.
    • La Pampa, 2000–2001: shows how pre-VIIRS months are estimated.

Extra mile

  • An experimental LightGBM model estimates the 24-hour probability of a critical hot spot per cell. It reaches ROC-AUC 0.92, and its “Extreme” class is 276 times better than chance.
  • A separate app feeds the model with Open-Meteo weather forecasts.
  • We evaluated the model with the same rigor and labeled its unproven parts as experimental.

Tools

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL.
  • Data and backend: pandas, DuckDB, Parquet, FastAPI, pytest.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL, TanStack Query, i18next, Tailwind, Vitest.
  • Prediction: LightGBM, scikit-learn.
  • Infrastructure: Docker, uv, GitHub.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER (MERRA-2), Open-Meteo, IGN Georef, CONAE, SNMF.
  • Hardware: standard laptops. No GPU is needed.

What makes it creative

  • Instead of a black-box model, we chose an auditable multiplication that anyone can redo by hand, and showed with data that it is accurate enough.
  • Every number states where it comes from: observed, mixed or estimated, with its range and confidence. Missing data is never shown as zero.
  • Learning is built into the product: guided case studies and the method dialog turn a data tool into an educational one.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: uncertainty on every estimate, coverage measured out of sample, and limitations published.
  • Data artifacts: sensor transitions (Terra only, then Terra + Aqua, then S-NPP, then NOAA-20), satellite outages, partial days, orbital drift of Terra and Aqua, and industrial heat sources.
  • Comparability: months are only compared within their own sensor era.
  • Accessibility: Spanish and English, phone layout, keyboard use.
  • Cost and reproducibility: no ML on the server, versioned data, fixed seeds and scripts that reproduce results byte for byte.
  • The team’s mix: our team includes a firefighter. Field experience shaped which questions the tool answers first.
